reconcile.connective: Defenders read the two laws as covering different cases: the light seven-day impurity for an accidental encounter, the karet penalty only for knowing, willful intercourse.

discrepancy.connective: Eve Levavi Feinstein argues the two rulings cannot be reconciled by intent because they stem from different Priestly strata: the author of Leviticus 15:24, from the older P source, treats the act as mere ritual impurity and was simply unaware of the Holiness school's later prohibition and karet penalty in Leviticus 20:18.

skeptic.name: Eve Levavi Feinstein
skeptic.work: Sex During Menstruation: From Impurity to Prohibition (TheTorah.com)
skeptic.attribution: Eve Levavi Feinstein (Ph.D., Hebrew Bible, Harvard), "Sex During Menstruation: From Impurity to Prohibition," TheTorah.com (2016)

excerpts.excerpt_text: In Lev 20:18, persons guilty of this are condemned to death; here only to a seven days' separation; because, in the former case, Moses speaks of the act when both the man and woman were acquainted with the situation: in the latter, he speaks of a case where the circumstance was not known till afterwards; at least, so it appears these two places should be understood, so as to be reconciled.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names BOTH conflicting verses (Lev 20:18 death vs Lev 15:24 seven days' separation) and states the harmonization explicitly via the knowledge distinction (acquainted with the situation vs not known till afterwards) and even uses the word 'reconciled' — the single strongest reconcile excerpt on the row.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on Leviticus 15:24
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this exact pair directly, distinguishing Lev 15:24 (offense unknown till afterwards, seven days' separation) from Lev 20:18 (both parties knowing, death/karet), 'so as to be reconciled.' Row-surfaced harmonizer keyed to the passage; Haley's coverage of this specific pair is unconfirmed.
